# PART 3 – Few clusters {#part-3-few-clusters .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 3
:::

::: notes
Part three takes the problem of the first session, few clusters of unequal weight, and asks what a Bayesian model does about it. The CR2 test repairs the standard errors after the fit. A Bayesian model has no such repair: the dependence of the years of a country has to be written into the model, and a posterior predictive check tells us whether it has been.
:::

## The dependence of the years {#the-dependence-of-the-years .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| label: d3-persistence-check
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.6
# The posterior predictive check of persistence: the correlation within
# countries between the residual of a country-year and that of the year
# before, in 1,000 datasets replicated from each of the four two-way models,
# against its value in the data (companion/_model-outputs/bayes_panel_ppc_draws.csv)
bayes_ppc_draws |>
  datawizard::data_modify(model = factor(model, levels = c("common", "slopes", "ar1", "both"),
                                         labels = c("one slope", "a slope for each country", "persistent errors",
                                                    "country slopes and persistence"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(persistence)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, fill = ncl_blue, alpha = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = persistence$observed[1], colour = d_red, linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(model), ncol = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "correlation of a residual with that of the year before", y = "replicated datasets") +
  theme_slide(12) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue, size = 11))
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
- "If the model fits, then replicated data generated under the model should look similar to observed data" [@GelmanEtAl2014BayesianDataAnalysis, p. 143]
- The statistic: the persistence of the residuals, `r fmt_num(persistence$observed[1], 2)` in the data (red line)
- With one slope, the replicated persistence has a median of `r fmt_num(persistence$rep_median[persistence$model == "common"], 2)`, and no replicated dataset reaches the observed value. A slope for each country fails as well, with a median of `r fmt_num(persistence$rep_median[persistence$model == "slopes"], 2)`
- The two models with persistent errors pass
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
A model that passes its computational checks may still fail to describe the data. The test is to let the fitted model generate new datasets and compare them with the real one on a statistic that matters, and Bayesian Data Analysis states the principle: replicated data should look like the observed data. The statistic here is the persistence of the residuals, the correlation of the first session, about a half in the data. Look at the top left. The model with one slope replicates a persistence near zero, slightly negative, and not one of its datasets reaches the observed value, because a model with independent errors cannot produce a country that stays above the expected value year after year. The model with a slope for each country fails too. Only the two models in which the errors persist from year to year reproduce the persistence in the data.
:::

## Persistent errors {#persistent-errors .smaller}

$$ e_{ct} = \phi\, e_{c,t-1} + \varepsilon_{ct}, \qquad \varepsilon_{ct} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) $$

::: {.small}
- The error of each year carries a fraction φ of the error of the year before, `ar(time = year, gr = cntry, p = 1, cov = TRUE)` in brms, under the prior normal(0, 0.5), which is centred on no persistence
- φ has a posterior median of `r fmt_num(ar1_phi$median, 2)` (95% credible interval `r fmt_num(ar1_phi$q2.5, 2)` to `r fmt_num(ar1_phi$q97.5, 2)`), and `r fmt_pct(persistence$p_ppc[persistence$model == "ar1"], 0)` of the replicated values of persistence lie above the observed one
- The slope moves and widens, to a median of `r fmt_num(ar1$median, 5)` (95% credible interval `r fmt_num(ar1$q2.5, 5)` to `r fmt_num(ar1$q97.5, 5)`): the likelihood compares each year with what the year before predicts, so the information comes more from the change from one year to the next
- With a slope for each country as well, φ stays at `r fmt_num(both_phi$median, 2)`, and the spread of the slopes shrinks to `r fmt_num(both_sd$median, 4)` (95% credible interval `r fmt_num(both_sd$q2.5, 5)` to `r fmt_num(both_sd$q97.5, 4)`), so that the countries are pooled almost completely
:::

::: notes
The failed check names the next model. Let the error of each year carry a fraction phi of the error of the year before, a first-order autoregressive process within each country, with a prior on phi centred on no persistence. The posterior puts phi at about three quarters, and the model passes the check. The slope moves as well as widening, because the likelihood now compares each year with what the year before predicts, so the information comes more from changes from one year to the next than from the level of a year against the decade mean of its country. And with both terms in the model, persistence and a slope for each country, the spread of the slopes nearly vanishes. With ten years for each country, the data distinguish only poorly between slopes that differ and departures that persist, and once the persistence is in the model, they leave little room for slopes that differ.
:::

## The slope across the models {#the-slope-across-the-models .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: d3-slope-intervals
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 2.9
# The slope of the reproduced specification by least squares with 95%
# confidence intervals under conventional and CR2 errors (squares), and its
# posterior median with a 95% credible interval under the four two-way models
# (circles), in points of share per point of unemployment
# (companion/_model-outputs/bayes_panel_summary.csv, the course panel)
tibble::tibble(
  label = c("Least squares, conventional errors", "Least squares, CR2 errors",
            "Posterior, one slope", "Posterior, persistent errors", "Posterior, a slope for each country",
            "Posterior, country slopes and persistence"),
  estimate = c(rep(inference_of("conventional", "b"), 2), common$median, ar1$median, slopes$median, both$median),
  low = c(ci_conventional[[1]], ci_cr2$CI_L, common$q2.5, ar1$q2.5, slopes$q2.5, both$q2.5),
  high = c(ci_conventional[[2]], ci_cr2$CI_U, common$q97.5, ar1$q97.5, slopes$q97.5, both$q97.5),
  kind = c("frequentist", "frequentist", rep("Bayesian", 4))
) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(label = factor(label, levels = rev(label))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = 100 * estimate, y = label, shape = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#9aa8b3") +
  ggplot2::geom_errorbar(ggplot2::aes(xmin = 100 * low, xmax = 100 * high), width = 0.25, orientation = "y",
                         colour = ink) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.8, colour = ncl_blue) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c(frequentist = 15, Bayesian = 16), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "points of share per point of unemployment", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(13) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "grey20"))
```

::: {.small}
- The model that passes the check, with persistent errors and a slope for each country, puts the average slope at **`r fmt_num(both$median, 5)`**, with a 95% credible interval from `r fmt_num(both$q2.5, 5)` to +`r fmt_num(both$q97.5, 5)`
- Its probability that the slope is negative is `r fmt_num(both$pd, 3)`, and that the slope is steeper than −0.001, a fall of at least one point of share for a rise of ten points of unemployment, `r fmt_num(both$p_beyond, 3)`
:::

::: notes
Here is the slope under every model of the session, in points of share for each point of unemployment. The two squares at the top are least squares: the conventional interval, clearly below zero, and the CR2 interval, which ends at zero. The circles are the four posteriors. The model with one slope sits with the conventional interval, because it shares its assumption. The three models that allow for the dependence all centre a little nearer zero, and their intervals end near zero. The model that passes the check puts the probability that the slope is negative at ninety-seven and a half per cent, and the probability of a fall of at least one point of share for ten points of unemployment at about ninety per cent. The two approaches agree on the main point: once the dependence of the years enters the analysis, the evidence for a negative slope is much weaker than the conventional fit suggests.
:::

## A probability and a threshold {#a-probability-and-a-threshold .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The CR2 test classes the reproduced specification as not significant at 5%, with p = `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "p"), 4)` on `r fmt_num(inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "df"), 2)` df, a margin of `r fmt_num(100 * (inference_of("cr2_satterthwaite", "p") - 0.05), 2)` of a percentage point
- "only a small change is required to move an estimate from a 5.1% significance level to 4.9%, thus moving it into statistical significance" [@GelmanStern2006DifferenceSignificantNot, p. 328]
- The posterior states the same evidence as a probability that the slope is negative, `r fmt_num(both$pd, 3)`, around a central value smaller than the least-squares slope, and it leaves to the reader the judgement of whether a probability of that size is enough for the claim
:::

::: notes
The two approaches differ in what each makes of that evidence. The test draws a line, and the reproduced specification falls on the side of not significant at five per cent, by four hundredths of a percentage point. Gelman and Stern pointed out how little separates the two sides of such a line: a small change moves an estimate from a significance level of five point one per cent to four point nine. The posterior draws no line. It states the evidence as a probability that the slope is negative, about ninety-seven and a half per cent here, around a central value smaller than the least-squares slope, and it leaves you to judge whether a probability of that size is enough for the claim. In your report this afternoon you state your own result under the errors that you declared, and this is the language for saying what it means.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – Persistence held fixed {#hands-on-2-persistence-held-fixed .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the workspace**, in the console:

1. Fit the two-way regression by generalised least squares, with the persistence held at a value of your choice:

   ```{.r}
   euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
   fit <- nlme::gls(mcosmo ~ unemp + cntry + factor(year), data = euframes,
                    correlation = nlme::corAR1(0.5, form = ~ year | cntry, fixed = TRUE))
   summary(fit)$tTable["unemp", ]
   ```
2. Run it with 0, 0.5, 0.8 and 0.95 in place of 0.5, and note the slope and its standard error each time. At 0 the fit is the least-squares slope of the reproduced specification
3. **Which of these comparisons is the claim about, and what does the posterior of φ say about the choice between them?** Two sentences for your notes
:::

::: notes
The frequentist twin of the model with persistent errors runs in a second, so you can do by hand what the posterior does by averaging. Fit the two-way regression by generalised least squares, with the persistence held at a value of your choice, and note the slope and its standard error. At nought you get the least-squares slope of the reproduced specification. As you raise the value towards one, the comparison shifts from the level of each year against the decade mean of its country towards the change from one year to the next, and the slope moves towards zero while its standard error grows. Then write two sentences: which of these comparisons is the claim, as the paper states it, about, and what does the posterior of phi, about three quarters, say about the choice between them? [state the time]
:::
